newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSIGHT - Aussie steadies as support survives again.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT - Aussie steadies as support survives again.

text.p: *Six-week support survived another downside attack in heavy two-way trade, needs $0.7775 at least to take pressure off
*Swiss and US banks among the sellers while Asian and local corporates were on the bid, should keep range intact for now
*World waiting nervously to see if Fed hikes US rates at today's meeting. Decision has mixed implications for AUD.
The currency would have to clear last week's US$0.7832 high to put the bearishness behind it and ignite a new uptrend to US$0.7900 and beyond.
By 8.30 am (2230 GMT) the local dollar had settled at US$0.7742/47 after bouncing from US$0.7725, to be steady on Monday's late US$0.7740/45.

It put in a mixed performance on the crosses, easing to 89.43/53 yen from 89.94/04 but firming to 1.3244/57 marks from 1.3151/64 late here Monday. This was a product of yen strength after Japan reported a huge April trade surplus and mark weakness on concerns over Germany's budget deficit.
The near term course on the crosses could well be set by what the Federal Reserve decides on U.S. rates tonight, which was one reason why the implications were mixed for the A$.
If the Fed did hike it could generally be expected to lift the U.S. dollar against the yen and mark -- a caveat is that a big selloff in U.S. stocks and bonds could see it actually retreat near term.

The local currency, as part of the dollar bloc, could be expected to follow any rally on the crosses but was likely to lose ground on the US$ itself as interest differentials on official short term rates narrowed to just 25 basis points.

A Fed hike would also be viewed as reducing the scope for a policy easing here, since another 0.5 point cut would take domestic rates below those in the U.S. for the first time since the dollar was floated in 1983.
Equally, silence from the Fed could be seen as providing scope for an easing here should, as some suspect, key wages data tomorrow and Thursday show private sector pressures are muted.

Dealers said there was much talk the Treasury had argued for a cut at the last RBA board meeting and the main RBA objection had been wages. Thus if the data are tolerable the bank might just be swayed by the argument. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
